When demand and supply both decrease, $Q^*$ unambiguously falls while $\Delta P^*$ depends on the relative magnitudes of the shifts (and the slopes). With linear curves, $\Delta P^* = (\Delta \text{supply shift} - \Delta \text{demand shift})/(\text{sum of slopes})$.

## Simplified explanation

Fewer people want gari and it costs more to make, so less is sold. Price could go either way.
hint: Two shifts in the same direction for quantity.

body: If both buyers and sellers of condensed tiger nut milk expect the prices of condensed tiger nut milk to rise in the near future, what will happen to condensed tiger nut milk prices and sales today? Illustrate your answers with the appropriate diagram(s). **[4 marks]**
answer:
- **Buyers** want to buy now before the price rises → **demand today increases** (shifts right).
- **Sellers** hold back stock to sell later at the higher price → **supply today decreases** (shifts left).

Both shifts push **price up**, so the **price today rises** for sure. Demand ↑ raises quantity but supply ↓ lowers it, so the **change in sales today is indeterminate**.

Diagram: $D_1 \to D_2$ (right), $S_1 \to S_2$ (left); the new equilibrium is higher, with quantity ambiguous.

> [!answer]
> Price rises today; quantity sold today may rise, fall or stay the same.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Expectations of future prices are a determinant of both demand and supply. Speculative behaviour by both sides makes the expected price rise partly self-fulfilling.

## Simplified explanation

Buyers rush to buy now and sellers wait, so the price goes up now. Whether more or less is sold depends on which effect is bigger.

body: What is the difference between **ordinal** utility and **cardinal** utility? Explain why the assumption of cardinal utility is not needed in order to rank consumer choices. **[4 marks]**
answer:
**Cardinal utility** assumes satisfaction can be **measured in units (utils)** so that the size of differences matters (e.g. a mango gives 20 utils, an orange 10, so the mango gives twice as much). **Ordinal utility** assumes consumers can only **rank** bundles (prefer A to B, or be indifferent), without measuring by how much.

To predict choices we only need to know which bundle the consumer **prefers**, the best affordable bundle. Any ranking is enough: indifference-curve analysis finds the optimum where the budget line is tangent to the highest indifference curve ($MRS = P_x/P_y$) using only the ordering. Any increasing transformation of a utility function gives the same choices, so the actual numbers carry no extra information.

> [!answer]
> Cardinal = measurable utils; ordinal = ranking only. Choice depends only on the ranking, so measurability is unnecessary.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cardinal utility underlies marginal utility analysis ($MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y$). Ordinal theory (Hicks–Allen) replaces MU ratios with the **MRS**, which is invariant to monotonic transformations of utility, so demand theory survives without measurable utility.

## Simplified explanation

You don't need to know how much you like tea in numbers to know you like it more than coffee; ranking is enough to choose.

body: Describe the **equal marginal principle**. Explain why this principle may not hold if increasing marginal utility is associated with the consumption of one or both goods. **[6 marks]**
answer:
**Equal marginal principle:** a consumer maximises utility by allocating income so that the **marginal utility per cedi is equal across all goods** and all income is spent:
$$\frac{MU_X}{P_X} = \frac{MU_Y}{P_Y}, \qquad P_X X + P_Y Y = M.$$
If $MU_X/P_X > MU_Y/P_Y$, moving a cedi from Y to X raises total utility; with **diminishing MU**, doing so lowers $MU_X$ and raises $MU_Y$ until the ratios are equal.

**With increasing MU:** shifting spending towards X makes $MU_X$ **rise** further, so the gap widens rather than closes. The equality point is then a **minimum, not a maximum** of utility, and the consumer does better by spending all income on one good (a **corner solution**). So the principle no longer identifies the optimum.

> [!answer]
> Optimum where MU/P is equal for all goods; it relies on diminishing MU. With increasing MU the equal-ratio point is not a maximum and the consumer specialises in one good.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The equi-marginal condition is a first-order condition; the second-order condition for a maximum requires diminishing MU (convex preferences). Increasing MU means non-convex preferences, so the tangency is a utility minimum and corner solutions are optimal.

## Simplified explanation

Normally each extra unit pleases you less, so you spread your money around. If each extra unit pleased you more, you'd spend everything on just one thing.
hint: Diminishing MU is what makes the ratios converge.

body:
The table reveals the amount of rice (X) and amount of cocoa (Y) that a nation can produce from its available resources.

| Basket | A | B | C | D | E | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rice | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| Cocoa | 15 | 14 | 12 | 9 | 5 | 0 |

(i) Illustrate the information in the table graphically. **[2 marks]**
(ii) Imagine a technology is developed that makes it possible to produce twice as much rice at all levels of cocoa. Sketch the new PPF. **[2 marks]**
(iii) Does the new PPF show economic growth? Why or why not? **[2 marks]**
(iv) On which of these curves will the opportunity cost of increasing cocoa production from 9 to 14 units be higher? **[2 marks]**
answer:
**(i)** Rice on the horizontal axis, cocoa on the vertical. Plot A(0, 15), B(1, 14), C(2, 12), D(3, 9), E(4, 5), F(5, 0): a curve bowed out from the origin (increasing opportunity cost).

**(ii)** New PPF: rice doubles at each cocoa level: (0, 15), (2, 14), (4, 12), (6, 9), (8, 5), (10, 0). The vertical intercept stays at 15 cocoa; the curve pivots outward along the rice axis.

**(iii)** **Yes.** The economy can now produce more rice for every cocoa level (and more of both), so the PPF has shifted outward: economic growth.

**(iv)** Cocoa 9 → 14:
- Original PPF: rice falls 3 → 1, opportunity cost = **2 units of rice**.
- New PPF: rice falls 6 → 2, opportunity cost = **4 units of rice**.

The opportunity cost is **higher on the new PPF**, because each unit of resources now produces more rice, so moving resources into cocoa sacrifices more rice.

> [!answer]
> New PPF = (0,15), (2,14), (4,12), (6,9), (8,5), (10,0); it shows growth; the 9→14 cocoa move costs 2 rice originally but 4 rice on the new curve.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Technical progress biased toward one good rotates the PPF outward along that good's axis. It raises the opportunity cost of the *other* good, measured in units of the improved good.

## Simplified explanation

With better rice technology, every shift of resources to cocoa means losing more rice than before.
hint: Double each rice figure, keep cocoa.

body:
The XYZ Company can sell its entire output for GH¢18 per unit. XYZ's total cost function is

$TC = 6 + 33Q - 9Q^2 + Q^3$

where Q represents units of output.

(a) Calculate the firm's (i) total revenue function, (ii) marginal revenue function, (iii) marginal cost function, (iv) average total cost function. **[6 marks]**
(b) Determine the output level that minimizes average total cost (ATC) and verify that at this output level, ATC intersects MC from below. **[6 marks]**
answer:
**(a)**
(i) $TR = 18Q$
(ii) $MR = 18$
(iii) $MC = \dfrac{dTC}{dQ} = 33 - 18Q + 3Q^2$
(iv) $ATC = \dfrac{6}{Q} + 33 - 9Q + Q^2$

**(b)** $\dfrac{dATC}{dQ} = -\dfrac{6}{Q^2} - 9 + 2Q = 0 \Rightarrow 2Q^3 - 9Q^2 - 6 = 0$. Solving numerically: $Q \approx 4.64$. Second derivative $\dfrac{12}{Q^3} + 2 > 0$, so this is a minimum.

At $Q \approx 4.64$: $ATC = 6/4.64 + 33 - 41.75 + 21.52 \approx 14.06$ and $MC = 33 - 83.51 + 64.57 \approx 14.06$. So **MC = ATC at the minimum of ATC**.

Below this output (e.g. $Q = 4$: $MC = 9$, $ATC = 14.5$) MC < ATC and ATC is falling; above it (e.g. $Q = 5$: $MC = 18$, $ATC = 14.2$) MC > ATC and ATC is rising. So MC cuts ATC **from below** at its minimum.

> [!answer]
> TR = 18Q; MR = 18; MC = 33 − 18Q + 3Q²; ATC = 6/Q + 33 − 9Q + Q²; ATC is minimised at Q ≈ 4.64 where ATC = MC ≈ 14.06, with MC rising through ATC from below.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In general $\dfrac{dATC}{dQ} = \dfrac{MC - ATC}{Q}$, so ATC is falling when $MC < ATC$, rising when $MC > ATC$, and stationary exactly where $MC = ATC$. Since MC is rising there, it crosses ATC from below. (Note: AVC alone is minimised at $Q = 4.5$, where $AVC = MC = 12.75$.)

## Simplified explanation

Average cost keeps falling while the extra unit costs less than the average, and starts rising once the extra unit costs more. The turning point is where they are equal, about 4.64 units.

body:
An economist has estimated the demand and supply functions for your firm's product as follows:

Demand function: $P = 80 - Q$ $\quad$ Supply function: $P = 20 + 2Q$

(a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity for your product. **[2 marks]**
(b) Assume that government decides to impose a market price of GH¢70. Explain the type of price legislation it is. **[2 marks]**
(c) Show exactly the problem this legislation causes to the market for your product. **[2 marks]**
(d) How much will the government spend to solve the problem identified in (c) above? **[2 marks]**
(e) Calculate the elasticity of demand for your product at the equilibrium. **[2 marks]**
(f) Based on the elasticity of demand, explain what you will do about your price if you want to increase total revenue. **[2 marks]**
(g) As part of efforts to boost domestic tax revenue mobilisation, the government has imposed a tax of ¢6 per unit. Show how this will affect the equilibrium price and quantity. **[2 marks]**
(h) Is it your firm or your consumers who will bear more of the tax? Calculate and use your knowledge of elasticity to explain the tax incidence. **[4 marks]**
(i) Calculate the amount of tax revenue the government will raise from this new policy. **[2 marks]**
answer:
**(a)** $80 - Q = 20 + 2Q \Rightarrow Q^* = 20$, $P^* = 60$.

**(b)** GH¢70 is **above** equilibrium, so it is a **price floor (minimum price)**.

**(c)** At $P = 70$: $Q_d = 80 - 70 = 10$; $Q_s = (70 - 20)/2 = 25$. **Surplus (excess supply) of 15 units.**

**(d)** To maintain the floor the government buys the surplus: $15 \times 70 = $ **GH¢1,050**.

**(e)** $Q = 80 - P$, $dQ/dP = -1$; $E_d = -1 \times 60/20 = $ **−3** (elastic).

**(f)** Demand is elastic, so **lower the price**: quantity rises proportionately more and TR increases.

**(g)** Supply with the tax (on sellers): $P = 26 + 2Q$. $80 - Q = 26 + 2Q \Rightarrow Q = 18$, $P_c = 62$; sellers receive $P_p = 56$.

**(h)** Consumers pay $62 - 60 = $ GH¢2 per unit (1/3); producers lose $60 - 56 = $ GH¢4 per unit (2/3). **The firm bears more**, because demand is more elastic than supply at equilibrium ($|E_d| = 3$ vs $E_s = 0.5 \times 60/20 = 1.5$): buyers can more easily switch away, so sellers absorb most of the tax. Consumers' share $= E_s/(E_s + |E_d|) = 1.5/4.5 = 1/3$.

**(i)** Revenue $= 6 \times 18 = $ **GH¢108**.

> [!answer]
> $P^* = 60$, $Q^* = 20$; price floor → surplus of 15 costing GH¢1,050; $E_d = -3$ → cut price; with tax $Q = 18$, $P_c = 62$, $P_p = 56$; firm bears 2/3; revenue GH¢108.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Tax incidence: the less elastic side bears more. Here supply is less elastic than demand, so producers bear 2/3. The floor creates excess supply that must be absorbed (government purchase, quotas) or it will not be sustained.

## Simplified explanation

Equilibrium is 20 units at 60. A price of 70 is a floor that leaves 15 unsold. Buyers are price-sensitive, so lower prices raise revenue, and the firm ends up paying most of the tax.
hint: A legal price above equilibrium is a floor.

body: A decrease in demand is shown as a:

options.text: movement from a higher point to a lower point on an existing demand curve.
options.hint: That is an increase in quantity demanded.

options.text: movement from a lower point to a higher point on an existing demand curve.
options.hint: That is a decrease in quantity demanded.

options.text: rightward shift of a demand curve.
options.hint: That is an increase in demand.

options.text: leftward shift of a demand curve.
options.hint: Correct. A decrease in demand shifts the whole curve left.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A change in **demand** (caused by income, tastes, related prices, expectations, number of buyers) shifts the curve; a decrease shifts it **left**. Movements along the curve are changes in quantity demanded.

## Simplified explanation

Less demand = the whole curve moves left.

body: There is too little of a good thing when its:

options.text: marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost.
options.hint: Correct. More units would add more benefit than cost.

options.text: marginal cost exceeds its marginal benefit.
options.hint: Then there is too much.

options.text: marginal cost equals its marginal benefit.
options.hint: That is the optimal amount.

Top of the line elastic, bottom inelastic.

body: Which of the following statements concerning the relationships between total product (TP), average product (AP) and marginal product (MP) is **not** correct?

options.text: AP continues to rise so long as TP is rising.
options.hint: Correct. False: AP starts falling (when MP < AP) while TP is still rising.

options.text: AP reaches a maximum before TP reaches a maximum.
options.hint: True.

options.text: TP reaches a maximum when the MP of the variable input becomes zero.
options.hint: True.

options.text: MP cuts AP at the maximum AP.
options.hint: True.

## Advanced explanation

TP keeps rising while MP > 0, but AP falls as soon as MP < AP, which happens before MP reaches zero. So AP peaks (where MP = AP) before TP peaks (where MP = 0).

body: Explain why the marginal cost (MC) curve intersects both the average variable cost (AVC) and the average total cost (ATC) curves at their minimum points. **[4 marks]**
answer:
It follows from the **marginal–average relationship**:
- When $MC <$ average cost, each additional unit costs less than the average, so it **pulls the average down**.
- When $MC >$ average cost, each additional unit costs more than the average, so it **pulls the average up**.
- Therefore the average stops falling and starts rising exactly where $MC =$ average: at the **minimum** of AVC and of ATC.

Because MC is rising (diminishing returns) in that range, it cuts both curves **from below**. AVC reaches its minimum at a lower output than ATC, since AFC keeps falling and delays the turn of ATC.

> [!answer]
> MC below the average pulls it down, above pulls it up, so MC = average at the average's lowest point (for both AVC and ATC).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

$\dfrac{d(AC)}{dQ} = \dfrac{MC - AC}{Q}$, so $AC$ is minimised where $MC = AC$. The same holds for AVC since MC is also the derivative of TVC.

## Simplified explanation

If your next test score is below your average, your average falls; if above, it rises. The average is lowest where the next score equals it.
hint: Think of a student's average mark when the next mark is above or below it.

body: Why would a monopolist never knowingly operate in the **inelastic** portion of its demand curve? Is it optimal for the monopolist to operate there? Why or why not? **[8 marks]**
answer:
In the inelastic range ($|E_d| < 1$), **marginal revenue is negative**: $MR = P(1 - 1/|E_d|) < 0$. So:
- **Raising price (cutting output) increases total revenue**, and
- cutting output also **lowers total cost**.
Profit therefore rises unambiguously by moving up the demand curve. Since a monopolist maximises profit where $MR = MC$ and $MC > 0$, MR must be positive, which only happens in the **elastic** range.

It is therefore **never optimal** to operate on the inelastic portion.

> [!answer]
> In the inelastic range MR < 0; reducing output raises revenue and cuts costs, so profit-maximising output (MR = MC > 0) is always in the elastic range.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The profit-maximising condition $MR = MC > 0$ implies $|E_d| > 1$. The **Lerner index** $(P - MC)/P = 1/|E_d|$ requires $|E_d| > 1$ for a sensible markup.

## Simplified explanation

Where demand is inelastic, the monopolist could charge more, sell less, earn more revenue and spend less on production, so it would never stay there.

body: Using appropriate diagram(s), explain how the monopolist decides what output to produce and the associated price to charge. **[4 marks]**
answer:
Diagram: downward-sloping demand (AR) curve; MR curve below it (twice as steep for linear demand); U-shaped ATC; MC cutting ATC at its minimum.

1. **Output:** produce $Q_m$ where $MR = MC$ (MC cutting MR from below).
2. **Price:** go up from $Q_m$ to the demand curve and read off $P_m$, the highest price buyers will pay for that output.
3. **Profit:** $(P_m - ATC) \times Q_m$, the rectangle between $P_m$ and ATC at $Q_m$.

Because $P_m > MR = MC$, the monopolist charges a price above marginal cost and produces less than a competitive industry would.

> [!answer]
> Choose Q where MR = MC; charge the price on the demand curve at that Q; profit = (P − ATC) × Q.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Unlike a competitive firm, the monopolist is a price maker: once it picks output, the demand curve determines price. The result is allocative inefficiency ($P > MC$) and a deadweight loss.

## Simplified explanation

Make the amount where extra revenue equals extra cost, then charge the most customers will pay for that amount.
hint: MR = MC, then read price off demand.

body: If economic profits were zero, would a monopolist ever stay in business? Why might it be possible for a monopolist to earn positive economic profits in the long run? **[4 marks]**
answer:
**Yes.** Zero economic profit means the firm earns a **normal profit**: revenue covers all costs, including the opportunity cost of the owner's resources. The owners do as well as in their best alternative, so there is no reason to leave.

A monopolist can earn **positive economic profits in the long run** because **barriers to entry** prevent new firms from entering and competing the profits away, e.g. legal barriers (patents, licences, government franchise), control of essential resources, economies of scale (natural monopoly), and high start-up costs or strategic deterrence.

> [!answer]
> Yes: zero economic profit = normal profit. Barriers to entry let monopoly profits persist in the long run.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In competitive markets, free entry drives long-run economic profit to zero. A monopoly's barriers block entry, so the profit rectangle can persist.

## Simplified explanation

Zero 'economic' profit still pays the owner a fair return, so the firm stays. Monopolies keep extra profit because others can't get into the market.
hint: Normal profit and barriers to entry.

body: Why is a monopoly a **price maker**, but a perfectly competitive firm a **price taker**? **[4 marks]**
answer:
A **monopolist** is the **only seller** of a product with no close substitutes. Its demand curve is the **market demand curve**, which slopes downward, so it can choose the price (accepting the quantity buyers will take at that price): it is a price maker.

A **perfectly competitive firm** is one of **very many** sellers of an **identical** product, each too small to affect market supply. Buyers have perfect information and can switch freely, so if it charges above the market price it sells nothing, and it can sell all it wants at the market price. Its demand curve is **horizontal** (perfectly elastic): it is a price taker.

> [!answer]
> Monopoly faces the downward-sloping market demand curve and can set price; a competitive firm is tiny relative to the market with a perfectly elastic demand curve, so it must accept the market price.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Market power is the ability to raise price above MC without losing all sales. It depends on the elasticity of the firm's own demand curve: infinite for the competitive firm, finite for the monopolist.

## Simplified explanation

The only seller can set the price. One small seller among thousands selling the same thing has to accept the going price.
hint: Compare the demand curves each firm faces.

body:
Compare and contrast the following:

(a) Microeconomics versus Macroeconomics **[5 marks]**
(b) Positive versus Normative Statements **[5 marks]**
(c) Quantity demanded versus change in demand **[5 marks]**
(d) Law of variable proportions and diminishing marginal utility **[5 marks]**
answer:
**(a)** **Microeconomics** studies individual units (households, firms, single markets): price determination, consumer and producer behaviour, resource allocation. **Macroeconomics** studies the economy as a whole: GDP, unemployment, inflation, growth, money, fiscal and monetary policy. Both use the same tools (scarcity, choice, models) and are linked: macro outcomes are the sum of micro decisions.

**(b)** **Positive** statements describe *what is* and can be tested (e.g. 'Ghana's inflation rate rose in 2022'). **Normative** statements say *what ought to be* and rest on value judgements (e.g. 'Government should reduce inflation'). Both are used in policy: positive analysis predicts consequences; normative judgement chooses among them.

**(c)** A change in **quantity demanded** is a **movement along** a demand curve caused only by a change in the good's own price. A change in **demand** is a **shift** of the whole curve caused by other determinants (income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, number of buyers). Both describe changes in buyers' purchases.

**(d)** The **law of variable proportions** (diminishing marginal returns) is a **production** concept: adding more of a variable input to a fixed input eventually reduces the marginal product of the variable input. **Diminishing marginal utility** is a **consumption** concept: as a person consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit eventually falls. Similarity: both say that additional units eventually add less, holding something fixed (fixed factors vs a given time period/tastes). Difference: one concerns physical output and underlies rising MC and upward supply; the other concerns satisfaction and underlies downward-sloping demand.

> [!answer]
> Micro = parts, macro = whole; positive = testable, normative = value-based; quantity demanded = movement (own price), demand = shift (other factors); diminishing returns (production) vs diminishing MU (consumption), both 'additional units add less'.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These distinctions organise introductory economics. Note the parallel in (d): diminishing returns → rising MC → upward-sloping supply; diminishing MU → downward-sloping demand.

## Simplified explanation

Small parts vs the whole; facts vs opinions; moving along vs shifting the curve; extra workers add less vs extra units please less.
hint: For each pair give a definition of both, then a similarity and a difference.

body:
Yell-O Yew-Boats, Ltd. produces a popular brand of pointy birds called Blue Meanies. Consider the demand and supply equations for Blue Meanies:

$Q_{d,x} = 150 - 2P_x + 0.001I + 1.5P_y$ and $Q_{s,x} = 60 + 4P_x - 2.5W$

where $Q_x$ is monthly per-family consumption of Blue Meanies, $P_x$ is the price per unit of Blue Meanies, $I$ is the median annual per-family income = ¢25,000, $P_y$ is the price per unit of Apple Bonkers = ¢5.00 and $W$ is the median per-worker wage rate = ¢8.60.

(a) What type of good is an Apple Bonker? **[1 mark]**
(b) What are the equilibrium price and quantity of Blue Meanies? Calculate the price elasticity of demand at equilibrium. **[4 marks]**
(c) Suppose that median per-family income increases by ¢6,000. What are the new equilibrium price and quantity of Blue Meanies? **[3 marks]**
(d) Suppose that in addition to the increase in median per-family income, collective bargaining by Blue Meanie workers resulted in a ¢2.40 hourly increase in the wage rate. What are the new equilibrium price and quantity? **[4 marks]**
(e) Suppose after the ¢2.40 increase in the hourly wage rate the government imposes a per-unit tax of ¢1.5. Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity, consumer and producer surplus and the revenue to the government. **[5 marks]**
(f) In a single diagram, illustrate your answers to parts b, c, d and e. **[4 marks]**
answer:
**(a)** The coefficient on $P_y$ is **+1.5**: a higher price of Apple Bonkers raises demand for Blue Meanies, so Apple Bonkers are a **substitute**.

**(b)** $Q_d = 150 - 2P + 25 + 7.5 = 182.5 - 2P$; $Q_s = 60 + 4P - 21.5 = 38.5 + 4P$.
$182.5 - 2P = 38.5 + 4P \Rightarrow P^* = ₵24$, $Q^* = 134.5$.
$E_d = -2 \times 24/134.5 \approx -0.357$ (inelastic).

**(c)** $I = 31{,}000$: $Q_d = 188.5 - 2P$. $188.5 - 2P = 38.5 + 4P \Rightarrow P = ₵25$, $Q = 138.5$.

**(d)** $W = 11.00$: $Q_s = 60 + 4P - 27.5 = 32.5 + 4P$. $188.5 - 2P = 32.5 + 4P \Rightarrow P = ₵26$, $Q = 136.5$.

**(e)** Tax on sellers: $Q_s = 32.5 + 4(P - 1.5) = 26.5 + 4P$. $188.5 - 2P = 26.5 + 4P \Rightarrow P_c = ₵27$, $Q = 134.5$; sellers receive $P_p = ₵25.50$.
- CS: demand choke price $= 188.5/2 = 94.25$; $CS = \tfrac12(134.5)(94.25 - 27) \approx ₵4{,}522.56$.
- PS: the pre-tax supply curve $Q_s = 32.5 + 4P$ meets the price axis at $P = -8.125$; $PS = \tfrac12(134.5)(25.5 + 8.125) \approx ₵2{,}261.28$.
- Government revenue $= 1.5 \times 134.5 = ₵201.75$.

**(f)** One diagram: $D_1$ (intercept 91.25 on the price axis, 182.5 on the quantity axis) and $D_2$ (94.25, 188.5); $S_1$ (price-axis intercept −9.63) and $S_2$ (−8.13) after the wage rise, and $S_3$ shifted up by 1.5 for the tax. Equilibria: (134.5, 24), (138.5, 25), (136.5, 26), (134.5, 27).

> [!answer]
> Substitute; P = 24, Q = 134.5, $E_d \approx -0.36$; after income rise P = 25, Q = 138.5; after wage rise P = 26, Q = 136.5; with tax $P_c = 27$, $P_p = 25.5$, Q = 134.5, CS ≈ 4,522.6, PS ≈ 2,261.3, tax revenue 201.75.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Income (positive coefficient → normal good) shifts demand right; a wage rise (input cost) shifts supply left; a per-unit tax drives a wedge between buyer and seller prices. Of the ₵1.5 tax, buyers pay ₵1 (27 vs 26) and sellers ₵0.5 (25.5 vs 26), since demand is less elastic than supply here. PS is measured to the supply curve's (negative) price intercept, as in the department's marking scheme diagram.

## Simplified explanation

Plug in the numbers, set demand equal to supply, and solve. Higher income raises price and quantity; higher wages raise price and cut quantity; the tax raises the buyer's price further.
hint: Substitute the given values to get linear equations in P only.
